procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 10, 1970 of the Madhya Pradesh High Court, Indore Bench in Cr. Appeal No. 94 of 1970, which enhanced the sentence imposed by the Sessions Judge.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants were convicted by the Additional Sessions Judge. They appealed to the Madhya Pradesh High Court, Indore Bench. The High Court maintained the conviction but enhanced the sentence under Section 423(1A) of the Code of Criminal Procedure from six months rigorous imprisonment to two years rigorous imprisonment.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, limited only to the question of whether the High Court was justified in enhancing the sentences. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision to enhance the sentence.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the order of the High Court enhancing the sentence of the appellants.

facts: The appellants were convicted for an offence under s. 325 read with s. 34 of the Indian Penal Code.
The Sessions Judge sentenced them to six months of rigorous imprisonment.
The High Court, exercising its powers, enhanced the sentence to two years of rigorous imprisonment.

The High Court justified the enhancement by noting the severity of the injuries, where one victim sustained three skull fractures and lost his power of speech, and considered the original sentence too lenient.
law: The Supreme Court will only interfere with a sentence if it is established that the sentence is 'harsh or unjust' in the facts and circumstances of the case.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the High Court's decision and found that it had properly considered the facts and circumstances, particularly the severity of the victim's injuries.
The Court agreed with the High Court's assessment that the original six-month sentence was lenient given the gravity of the harm caused.
The appellants failed to provide any evidence or argument to suggest that the enhanced two-year sentence was unjust or harsh.
The Court concluded that the High Court's exercise of its power to enhance the sentence was justified and did not suffer from any 'infirmity or lack of appreciation of facts'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal and refused to interfere with the High Court's order because the appellants did not show that the enhanced sentence of two years was unjust or harsh, which is the required standard for the Supreme Court's intervention. The Court found the High Court was justified in increasing the sentence due to the severe nature of the injuries inflicted.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should interfere with the order of the High Court enhancing the sentence of the appellants.
appellant_arguments: The sentence should be reduced to the period already served (10 months) based on the facts and circumstances of the case.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's arguments are not explicitly stated in the text. However, their position is reflected in the High Court's reasoning, which the Supreme Court upheld. The argument would be that the High Court was justified in enhancing the sentence because the original sentence of six months was too lenient given the severity of the injuries inflicted (one victim sustained three skull fractures and lost the power of speech). The enhanced sentence was not unjust or harsh, and therefore did not warrant interference from the Supreme Court.

cases.case_name: Surta & Ors. v. State of Haryana
cases.principle: The Supreme Court interferes with a sentence only when it is established that the sentence is harsh or unjust in the facts and circumstances of the case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The Supreme Court will only interfere with a sentence when it is established that the sentence is harsh or unjust in the facts and circumstances of the case.
obiter: Consideration of age has sometimes occasioned interference with a sentence.
There are instances of interference in sentences in cases of violation of statutory offences.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court will not interfere with a sentence passed by a lower court unless it is established that the sentence is harsh or unjust in the facts and circumstances of the case. In this instance, the High Court was justified in enhancing the sentence because the original sentence was lenient given the severity of the injuries caused to one of the victims, who sustained three skull fractures and lost the power of speech. The enhanced sentence was not shown to be unjust or harsh.
legal_tests_applied: This Court interferes with sentence only when it is established that the sentence is harsh or unjust in the facts and circumstances of the case.
why_appellant_lost: The appellants failed to establish that the sentence passed by the High Court was unjust or harsh.
The High Court's exercise of its power to enhance the sentence did not suffer from any infirmity or lack of appreciation of the facts.
The High Court was justified in observing that the sentence passed by the trial court was lenient in the circumstances of the case, given the severity of the injuries.
why_respondent_won: The High Court was justified in holding that in view of the severity of the injuries caused to one of the victims—who sustained three fractures on his skull and totally lost his power of speech—the sentence passed by the trial court was lenient.
The sentence passed by the High Court was not shown to be unjust or harsh, which is the standard required for the Supreme Court to interfere.
policy_considerations: Any interference has to be supported by rules and principles in the administration of justice.
